entries.title: Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
entries.summary: A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing dozens of people and trapping many under rubble. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.
entries.content:
Colombia

Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100

Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026

A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing dozens of people and trapping many under rubble. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.

Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

What is the latest?

Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.

He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.

"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."

What's happening on the ground?

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, later said that at least 27 people had died in the quake.

Officials in Risaralda said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.

And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.

The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were four dead and 69 wounded in her district as of late morning local time.

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.

What do we know about the quake's size and location?

The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors. 

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

entries.title: Why the Rhine drought is bad news for Germany's recovery
entries.summary: Germany’s inland waterways still move around 5% of the nation's goods. With the Rhine at a critically low level, DW explores how the drought is hitting the economy where it hurts most.
entries.content:
August 10, 2026

Germany’s inland waterways still move around 5% of the nation's goods. With the Rhine at a critically low level, DW explores how the drought is hitting the economy where it hurts most.

Water levels on the Rhine River — a small but critical artery for goods vital to Germany’s industry — remain critically low as a result of weeks of drought.

At one of the river's shallowest stretches, Kaub — between Mainz and Koblenz — the water level stood at around 16 centimeters (6.3 inches) at Monday lunchtime, according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration (WSV).

Although the real navigable channel is roughly a meter deeper, 40 centimeters is regarded as the lowest for standard commercial vessels at Kaub.

Ship operators use the reading at Kaub to decide how much cargo their barges can safely carry and whether a passage is feasible at all.

According to local media, in recent weeks, carriers have significantly cut their cargoes along the Rhine — in many cases to as little as one-fifth of normal capacity.

The problem isn't just limited to the Middle Rhine, the 130-kilometer (80-mile) stretch between Mainz and Bonn that is the narrowest and shallowest section of the river.

Areas around Cologne, Düsseldorf, Duisburg-Ruhrort and Emmerich are also at historic lows.

Jens Schwanen, the head of the BDB association of inland shipping, told the Rheinische Post newspaper on Monday that the Rhine may become impassable at Kaub before the end of the week.

This would effectively split the river in two for commercial traffic.

What effect will the drought have on the German economy?

The drought could not come at a worse time for Germany’s economy, which is already grappling with weak growth, high energy costs and fading industrial competitiveness.

Germany still relies on its long rivers and waterways to transport some 5% of goods around the country, most of them bulk materials, including iron ore, coal, sand and petroleum products.

Out of 3.28 billion tons of goods transported in 2024, 173 million tons were carried by inland water, including the Rhine, according to BDB.

Eurostat, the European Union's statistics agency, calculated in 2023 that the Rhine corridor — from the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands to the German-Swiss border — accounts for around 40% of freight by ton-kilometers.

After two previous droughts, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated in 2023 that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.

In an economy that has barely grown for the past two years, even a temporary 1% hit to industrial output is highly damaging.

The German Economic Institute (IW) now predicts a 0.4% drop in gross domestic product, effectively wiping out this year's economic growth, which was expected at 0.5%.

"A prolonged disruption of navigability on the Rhine could completely stifle the tiny seed of growth we have," warned IW economist Thilo Schäfer in an interview with Bild newspaper last week.

Other experts have warned of losses of €1 to €2 billion ($1.2 to $2.3 billion) in the third quarter alone, with the steel, chemicals and energy sectors hit especially hard.

What happens if the River Rhine is effectively split in two?

The BDB's Schwanen warned that "due to the lack of rainfall, a single-digit reading is forecast for the first time this week at the Kaub gauge."

"In principle, this means the Rhine is no longer navigable along its entire length and is therefore effectively divided in two," he told the Rheinische Post.

This would result in two separate areas. On the one hand, shipping traffic would continue between the North Sea ports of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Antwerp and the Cologne region via the Rhine and the Western German canal system.

Further south, shipping would operate on the tributaries of the Neckar, Moselle, and Main, as well as the Main-Danube Canal, which is regarded as a key global link on the route to and from Southeast Europe.

Between the two sections, shipping companies would then try to move cargo onto trucks and freight rail services.

However, Germany's roads cannot absorb the typical 50 to 150 truckloads that a single large barge can handle without severe congestion and substantially higher costs.

Baden-Württemberg said Monday it would join four other German states in easing restrictions on truck movements on Sundays to help ease congestion.

Following urgent talks last Thursday, Transport Minister Steffen Bilger announced several other measures to shore up Germany's supply chain.

These include cutting red tape for heavy loads shifted to the road network, stopping unnecessary roadworks and better coordination with DB Cargo, the rail freight arm of Deutsche Bahn.

Are regular droughts a new reality for Europe's waterways?

Extremely low water on the Rhine and other major European rivers used to be rare events.

Yet, many scientists believe climate change is now making them more frequent, longer and more severe.

According to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, western Europe has just experienced its warmest June and July on record, with exceptionally low rainfall driving much lower than average water levels on the Rhine, Danube and Seine.

The current crisis marks the third major low‑water episode in eight years, after major droughts in 2018 and 2022.

The Rhine has traditionally been supported during dry summer months by meltwater from Alpine snow and glaciers. As those glaciers retreat and snow cover declines, this natural buffer is weakening.

Germany’s Federal Institute of Hydrology (BfG) projected in 2023 that severe low-water events like 2018 could strike every five to 10 years by mid-century.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

entries.title: India news: Jharkhand police use tear gas, water cannons to disperse student protesters
entries.summary: Police used force to disperse students marching towards the Jharkhand assembly, as protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams entered their third week. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India: Jharkhand police use tear gas on student protesters

Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026

Police used force to disperse students marching towards the Jharkhand assembly, as protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams entered their third week. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us.

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Monday, August 10:

  • Police used water cannons to disperse the crowd of students marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi
  • TG Mohandas was arrested in Kerala over remarks he allegedly made about the women at the student protests last month
  • Multiple reports indicate that young women involved in the Cockroach Janta Party-led movement are facing severe online harassment
  • Model Rhiya Ahir speaks out after online abuse over protest
  • Court calls sexual harassment allegations against former wrestling chief 'fabricated'

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Thanks for reading!

Thanks for reading!

That's all for today, people!

I will be back tomorrow with more.

Cheers!

Skip next section Assam flood toll climbs to 100

Assam flood toll climbs to 100

The situation in India's northeastern Assam state remained critical on Monday, with the death toll in the floods reaching 100, officials said.

Two more people died overnight on Sunday after weeks of heavy monsoon rain inundated villages, damaged roads and farmland and disrupted livelihoods.

More than 700,000 people have been displaced since the floods began last month, while about 49,000 remain in 125 relief camps and distribution centers, officials said.

Authorities are warning that, several rivers, including the Brahmaputra, remained above danger levels, raising the risk of further flooding in vulnerable areas.

Farukuddin Ahmed, a 47-year-old trader from Nazira town in Assam's worst-hit Sivasagar district, that in a nearby village of 100 houses only a few remain.

"The residents, mainly dairy farmers, have to rebuild their lives from scratch having lost all their cattle," he said, according to the Associated Press.

Authorities are assessing the damage and providing financial assistance to affected residents. According to the government about 50,000 people had already received interim compensation.

While flooding is a recurring problem in Assam during the monsoon, experts warn that climate change is making rainfall increasingly erratic and extreme.

Skip next section Jharkhand student protests: Police use water cannons to disperse marching students

Jharkhand student protests: Police use water cannons to disperse marching students

Police used tear gas, batons and water cannons to disperse the crowd of students marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi in the eastern state of Jharkhand on Monday, reports said. 

On Sunday, the sixth round of talks between student protesters and the government failed to reach a breakthrough after students alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams.

The sit-in protests in Jharkhand began on July 25.

Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto has been on an indefinite hunger strike since August 2 is demanding action over alleged irregularities in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC), Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission Combined Graduate Level (JSSC CGL) and other competitive examinations required to qualify for government jobs.

Meanwhile, authorities on Monday arrested former Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) chairperson L Khiangte in connection with alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations, reports said.

Earlier, Chief Minister Hemant Soren has assured the protesting students that his government would take action over alleged exam irregularities and invited them for talks.

Skip next section Court calls sexual harassment allegations against former wrestling chief 'fabricated'

Court calls sexual harassment allegations against former wrestling chief 'fabricated'

A Delhi court called the sexual harassment allegations against former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh "false and fabricated" and part of a "deep conspiracy which seems to be politically motivated," media reports said.

Singh was acquitted last week of the sexual harassment and stalking charges brought by female athletes. The former lawmaker from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), had denied allegations that he groped wrestlers and demanded sexual favors.

In its detailed judgment, the court cited "material contradictions" in the wrestlers’ accounts, inconsistencies between their allegations and documentary evidence, and the absence of contemporaneous complaints, media reports said.

The court said some allegations appeared "rehearsed, well-practiced and planted."

Lawyer Rebecca John, who represented four of the women, described the acquittal as "deeply, deeply disturbing" on Monday, news channel NDTV reported.

The allegations had triggered months of protests in New Delhi in 2023, led by prominent Indian wrestlers with hundreds joining the sit-in demonstrations accusing authorities of failing to act against Singh.

Delhi police charged Singh in 2023, and a court formally brought charges against him in 2024 over allegations involving five women.

Skip next section Rhiya Ahir speaks out after online abuse over protest

Rhiya Ahir speaks out after online abuse over protest

Mumbai-based model Rhiya Ahir, who gained attention after standing in front of a police van carrying protesters during last month's Cockroach Janta Party-led demonstrations, has spoken about facing online abuse and threats following the protest.

In an interview with DW's Shalu Yadav, Ahir said the attention had come at a "heavy price" of online trolling and harassment, adding that women should be able to express their views without being targeted.

She referred to comments made about women protesters, including comments that they "should be raped" and would "enjoy it," saying such remarks could influence others and should not be allowed to go unchallenged.

"I read one comment saying 'we are going to rip you apart from the middle. And nobody's going to come to lay flowers on your grave,'" she said.

Ahir described the attacks as "criminal."

"I will not let it slide," she said. "I will not let them feel that they can sit behind their blank screens and feel so powerful by belittling other people.

Her comments come amid a wider online campaign targeting women who took part in the CJP-led protests, with reports of fake and AI-manipulated images, doxxing and threats against participants.

Skip next section Right-wing commentator arrested over sexual assault remarks targeting protesters

Right-wing commentator arrested over sexual assault remarks targeting protesters

An activist who considers himself a right-wing "political commentator" was arrested in the southern state of Kerala on Sunday over remarks he allegedly made about the women at the Cockroach Janta Party-led student protests last month, media reports said.

The case was registered following a complaint alleging that videos on TG Mohandas' YouTube channel, Pathrika, were intended to disturb public order and create fear and unrest.

According to reports, in the videos, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi protests could lead to gang rape and claimed that women attending it "like rape" and that some "enjoy being raped."

He also called for police to open fire at protesters.

News channel NDTV reported that Mohandas is a former member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). However, the RSS has denied any association with the commentator.

The BJP on Monday criticized the arrest as "discriminatory" and accused the Kerala government of attempting to divert attention from other issues, reports said.

Women protesters being targeted online

The development comes amid an online campaign targeting women who took part in CJP-led student protests. The countrywide stir ended last month with the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Multiple reports indicate that young women involved in the movement are facing severe online harassment. They have been targeted with fake and AI-manipulated images, as well as a barrage of online abuse, including assault threats.

Additionally, their phone numbers and home addresses have been leaked online alongside targeted attacks against their family members.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

Female protesters who took part in Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demonstrations against the government are facing harassment and doxxing. In the latest development, a right-wing activist was arrested in the southern state of Kerala for allegedly posting a video saying that those attending the protests "like rape."

Meanwhile, a Delhi court has said allegations of sexual harassment made by women wrestlers against former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh were "false" and "fabricated."

For all this and more, stay tuned to our blog.

entries.title: Which country is the new Mecca defense pact targeting?
entries.summary: Observers suggest the new alliance between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan won't result in any of the countries fighting for each other. Instead it's about preventing Iran and Israel from regional dominance, they say.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Which country is the new Mecca defense pact targeting?

August 10, 2026

Observers suggest the new alliance between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan won't result in any of the countries fighting for each other. Instead it's about preventing Iran and Israel from regional dominance, they say.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia sealed a historic defense pact on Friday, signing an agreement "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The so-called "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement" between the three Sunni Muslim-majority states is meant to increase cooperation during regional uncertainty and threats from the Iran war.

The agreement was signed in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

The alliance has been likened to a NATO-style alliance and on Friday, the Pakistani foreign ministry said that an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all.

But experts and analysts have been quick to point out that the deal is unlikely to work that way — at least at first.

For example, on the weekend the Houthi rebel group in Yemen fired at Saudi Arabian oil facilities again. The Houthis consider Saudi Arabia their enemy and are also aligned with Iran. The latter has also targeted Saudi Arabia after the US and Israel attacked it, starting a war in late February, because it sees the Saudis as a US ally.

But following the Houthi attack on the weekend, neither Turkey nor Pakistan sprang to the Saudis' defense. Nor are they likely to attack Iran, analysts say. In fact, Pakistan is acting as a mediator between Iran and the US currently.

Mecca agreement an 'elastic defense pact'

This arrangement is meant as more of a deterrent and as an "elastic defense pact," Dania Thafer, executive director of the Washington-based think tank the Gulf International Forum, or GIF, told DW late last week.

"If you look at the parties in this agreement, you have Saudi Arabia, which is in the middle of this conflict. But you also have Turkey and Pakistan, who both have relations with Iran and both have relations with the US. So I think it's an extra layer of deterrence, if you will, for Saudi Arabia," Thafer explained. "I think Saudi Arabia is looking at a layered deterrence approach to regional threats as they emerge."

This new alliance is likely to work out in various stages with the short-term goal being a "stabilized region," Kamran Bokhari, a senior fellow at the Middle East Policy Council in Washington, told DW.

Technology transfer and investment

Longer term goals will involve defense cooperation rather than fighting, other experts have said.

"The three countries complement each other unusually well," Andreas Krieg, a lecturer in security at King's College London, told news agency Agence France-Presse last week.

Saudi Arabia has oil wealth but limited defense technology and has been reliant on the US up until now. Meanwhile Turkey and Pakistan need investment and have strong armed forces, and in Turkey's case an advanced defense-industrial sector, Krieg explained. Pakistan is the only one with nuclear weapons of the three.

"Turkey has technology and production capacity but needs markets and investment. Pakistan has a workforce, military institutions and nuclear deterrent, but needs financing and industrial capabilities," Krieg noted.

Who does the Mecca pact target?

A Turkish official cited by Reuters said the agreement was purely defensive in nature and open to any regional neighbors who might want to sign on. Egypt is thought to be a potential partner but also has other allies to consider, including the United Arab Emirates. The latter have not joined and relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia are currently strained.

The Turkish official also said the pact does not replace or negate previous bilateral or multilateral agreements between signatories, nor is it directed at any one actor or threat.

Yet there's no doubt the agreement has been understood as a deterrent, mainly against two other nations, Iran and Israel.

The Mecca pact's objectives are not about some kind of military victory, Khalid al-Jaber, director of the Doha-based Middle East Council on Global Affairs wrote in a Sunday op-ed for Qatari news outlet, Al Jazeera. "It is the prevention of hegemony."

"Diminished American weight could leave the region inside an order whose rules are set by two actors alone: Israel and Iran," he continued. "The Mecca pact is best understood as an early attempt to build a third pole — a bloc that does not need to fight either power, but one that has enough weight to deny either a monopoly over the region."

How does Israel feel about it?

Two of the signatories to the agreement — Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — don't recognize Israel and have no official relations with it, even though at least in Saudi Arabia's case there are likely some covert ties. Turkey does recognize Israel but the relationship is strained at the moment, due to Israel's activity in Gaza that Turkey has called genocide.

Turkish leader Erdogan said last week that Israel's actions in Syria and Lebanon also constitute a threat to Turkish security.

"The development [of the Mecca pact] poses significant challenges for Israel, pushes the prospect of normalization with Riyadh further out of reach and cuts short the vision of a 'new Middle East'," Oshrit Birvadker, a research fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, wrote in a Saturday editorial for the outlet Israel Hayom.

Birvadker also believes that the new trilateral alliance will increase the growing rivalry and tensions between Turkey and Israel.

Mixed reactions in Iran

The Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University looked at how the Iranians were reacting.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi did not seem too upset by the agreement. On the social media platform, X (formerly Twitter) he posted that "when Muslims stand together, we can face every challenge by malicious outsiders head-on."

Observers took this to be a positive, part of Iran's argument for pushing the US out of the region.

Some Iranian observers thought that the Saudis might be trying to leverage the better relations that the Turkish and Pakistanis have with the Iranians, to make itself safer from Iranian attacks. But other Iranian politicians were more critical, saying that Saudi Arabia wasn't safe with the US as an ally and wouldn't be safe with Turkey and Pakistan either.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: How climate change is reshaping Africa's malaria risk
entries.summary: Researchers say warming temperatures are altering malaria transmission patterns across Africa, creating new challenges for health systems and disease control.
entries.content:
August 10, 2026

Researchers say warming temperatures are altering malaria transmission patterns across Africa, creating new challenges for health systems and disease control.

For decades, global efforts towards the eradication of malaria, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, have focused essentially on West and Central Africa, where the disease is most endemic.

The WHO African Region accounts for about 95% of global malaria cases and deaths. More than half of all malaria deaths in the region occur in Nigeria (31.9%), the Democratic Republic of Congo (11.7%) and Niger (6.1%). Children under 5 years of age account for about 76% of malaria deaths in the region.

To stem the tide of malaria cases across Africa, the global health body has recommended a wider use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine among children living in regions with moderate to high malaria transmission by the Plasmodium falciparum — a parasite that causes 95% of all malaria infections in Africa. It's transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

The WHO warned in April 2025 that recent funding cuts were jeopardising malaria control efforts, with more than half of malaria-endemic countries surveyed reporting moderate or severe disruptions to malaria services.

A study published in The Lancet found that the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine reduced all-cause mortality among vaccine-eligible children by 13.2% in pilot programs in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.

A changing disease landscape

Malaria transmission is most efficient within temperature ranges common across many tropical regions of West and Central Africa, according to a new study published in the journal Nature.

Malaria transmission by mosquitoes usually peaks at temperatures of around 25 degrees Celsius (77 Fahrenheit) and becomes much less likely when temperatures drop below 16 degrees or rise above 34 degrees Celsius, largely because the malaria parasite must complete part of its life cycle inside the mosquito — a process that is highly temperature-dependent.

Because of this, malaria transmission has historically been most favourable across many tropical parts of West and Central Africa, where temperatures frequently fall within the range most suitable for transmission.

In contrast, some parts of Southern Africa and the highlands of East Africa have historically remained cool enough to keep the spread of malaria at bay, preventing the disease from becoming a major public health burden.

That, however, is beginning to change. The Nature study found that rising temperatures are making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for malaria transmission, while parts of West Africa are becoming too hot for optimal transmission.

What does this mean for the continent?

Climate change is not only heating up the continent, it's redistributing risks, says Olugbenga Mokuolu, professor of pediatrics at Nigeria's University of Ilorin.

Although West African countries like Nigeria fall under areas that are "too hot for malaria to thrive, this is not good news to celebrate either, because a world that's too hot for malaria is not a good world for children's health overall," Mokuolu, who also serves as an advisor to the Nigerian Minister of Health on malaria elimination, told DW.

"The same heat that's inconvenient for mosquitoes is dangerous for people," he added, noting that climate is "not the primary driving factor of malaria. Funding, drug and insecticide resistance, and health system strength still matter more."

Olugbenga continued that the elimination and prevention of malaria on the continent could become "a story of two very different regions: West and Central Africa may get a small, unplanned assist from climate, while East and Southern Africa, historically lower-burden areas, face a growing new threat that could undo hard-won gains."

Are African health systems keeping pace?

Climate change is fundamentally changing the geography of disease on the continent, Olumide Idowu, founder of the International Climate Change Development Initiative, told DW.

Idowu added that many African countries have developed adaptation plans but implementation has lagged behind the pace of climate change.

Although Africa is one of the lowest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions, it remains one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change — posing systemic threats to the economy, infrastructure, and even its fragile health systems.

Idowu mentioned that without a significant increase in "investment at home, reinforcement of local institutional capacity and embedding health as a core pillar of climate resilience, many African countries risk being unprepared for the changing epidemiological landscape that climate change is creating."

The regions expected to be hardest hit are also regions less accustomed to fighting malaria today, the study revealed.

"Governments, health systems and communities must adapt to this evolving threat, including getting ready now to run more aggressive anti-malaria programs in cooler areas where risk is rising," Olugbenga said.

He also urged countries in West and Central Africa to sustain malaria elimination efforts, warning that resistance to insecticides and drugs, funding gaps and weak health systems could easily negate any reduction in malaria transmission associated with rising temperatures.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Middle East: Iran wants US concessions before opening Hormuz
entries.summary: Iran's Foreign Ministry reiterated that the US must meet Tehran's demands before the Strait of Hormuz is reopened. Meanwhile, Germany says Trump's plan for Gaza could get Hamas to put down its weapons. DW has more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Middle East: Iran wants US concessions before opening Hormuz

Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026

Iran's Foreign Ministry reiterated that the US must meet Tehran's demands before the Strait of Hormuz is reopened. Meanwhile, Germany says Trump's plan for Gaza could get Hamas to put down its weapons. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Iran won't reopen Strait of Hormuz until US meets its demands to end war
  • Tehran says ships will be expected to pay for transit through the narrow waterway
  • In other news from the Middle East, Germany says the US plan for Gaza could help disarm Hamas

Keep reading for the latest developments in the war in Iran and wider conflict in the Middle East from Monday, August 10.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Trump says if Iran is demanding compensation, then he is too

Trump says if Iran is demanding compensation, then he is too

President Donald Trump said on Monday that the US would demand compensation from Iran, in response to Tehran saying it would seek compensation over US and Israeli attacks.

Over the weekend, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over new shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz. But it said that reopening the waterway would depend on Washington meeting various conditions — including an end to sanctions, military threats and an agreement on compensation for damages resulting from the war.

Trump said that this was "never mentioned" in any negotiations with the US to date.

"But is an interesting idea because now ‌I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

He cited specifically a 2000 terrorist suicide bombing of the USS Cole ship, but alleged there were "thousands of others killed in combat."

Trump's remarks come a day after he said he was not engaging in major talks with Iran, telling US media outlet Axios that the US was "low-keying" its approach.

The US and Iran have frequently put out vastly contradictory claims and counterclaims about the status and details of their talks and terms.

Skip next section Iranian supreme leader calls for 'unity,' president says

Iranian supreme leader calls for 'unity,' president says

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that he had a nearly seven-hour meeting with Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.

He did not, however, say exactly when or where they met.

Pezeshkian told the state-run IRIB that he and Khamenei discussed "people’s livelihoods, the state of the market, employment, people's housing." He said they also talked about "problems that are now being created as a result of the sanctions."

Most important, Pezeshkian said, was the importance Khamenei put on "unity and cohesion."

"All of the enemy's plans are aimed at creating division," Pezeshkian said. "What we have to do is prevent divisions from emerging."

It is only the second time the Iranian president said he has met with the supreme leader since Khamenei was appointed in March. He came to power after a US-Israeli strike killed his father. Khamenei, believed to have been wounded in the same attack, has not appeared in public since then.

Skip next section Germany says US plan for Gaza could lead towards disarmament of Hamas

Germany says US plan for Gaza could lead towards disarmament of Hamas

The German government regards US President Donald Trump's plan for ‌Gaza as an opportunity to make progress towards the disarmament of Hamas, a Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Monday.

Asked about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's announcement Sunday that Israel rejected the US-led plan, the spokesperson said some disagreement was not surprising.

"With such a ‌complex undertaking, it was perfectly clear there ⁠would be many, many ⁠unanswered questions," he added.

Late last month, Trump hailed a 15-point plan that would see Hamas lay down its weapons and the Israeli military withdraw from the Gaza Strip. It expands on an October 2025 ceasefire agreement that slowed, but did not end, the conflict in the Palestinian territory, about two-thirds of which is under Israeli control.

Despite the truce, Israel continued to carry out airstrikes in Gaza. Health officials there say more than 1,200 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed since October 2025. Five Israeli soldiers were killed in Gaza during that time. Hamas, which is classified as a terrorist organization by Israel, the US, Germany and several countries, does not disclose figures on its war dead.

On Sunday, Netanyahu said Israeli troops would not leave the Gaza Strip until Hamas had been "genuinely" disarmed.

Skip next section Iran demands concessions from US before reopening Strait of Hormuz

Iran demands concessions from US before reopening Strait of Hormuz

An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Iran would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States meets its conditions.

"It is up to the US side to stop and make amends for its illegal and destructive actions," Esmail Baghaei said Monday.

What are Iran's demands on the US?

In a statement over the weekend, a member of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and Revolutionary Guards commander said Tehran had the following demands of the US:

  • Never to threaten Iran again
  • Pay compensation for months of war damage
  • Permanently end its war against Iran and its allies in the region, namely Lebanese militants Hezbollah; Houthi rebels in Yemen; and Hamas in the Gaza Strip
  • Lift its blockade of Iranian ports and ships in the Strait of Hormuz and pull its military out of the area
  • Lift sanctions and release frozen Iranian assets 

The impasse over the Strait of Hormuz has led to a global jump in fuel prices.

Iran is holding talks with Oman over transit through the strait, including a possible temporary shipping corridor, but it has said any actual reopening depends on negotiations with the United States.

On Sunday, however, US President Donald Trump said the US is not engaged in major talks with Iran.

"We are low-keying it," he said, according to US media outlet Axios. "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money."

Trump also expressed his optimism that a satisfactory conclusion would eventually be reached.

"It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," he said of the war.

Skip next section Tehran: Ships will be expected to pay for transit through the narrow waterway

Tehran: Ships will be expected to pay for transit through the narrow waterway

Iran has said it intends to charge commercial vessels for passage through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement Monday from the Foreign Ministry. 

Iranian media cited spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying that Iran was working with Oman on "mechanisms for monitoring security, protecting the environment and combating crime at sea." 

Fees would be for maritime services provided to ships, he explained.

The dispute over transit rights in the strait, through which some 20% of the world's oil passed before the war and which is a key route for gas and fertilizer, is regarded as a key reason behind the continuation of the war against Iran.

Before the United States and Israel launched the conflict against Iran at the end of February, shipping through the waterway did no incur tolls nor fees for transit.

The Strait of Hormuz measures only around 39 kilometers (24 miles) at its narrowest point.

Since Iran and Oman each claim the maximum 12 nautical miles allowed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) as their territorial waters, there are no international waters in the narrowest part of the roughly 21-nautical-mile-wide strait.

The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees a right of transit passage and prohibits a blockade of commercial vessels. Iran, however, does not accept this legal position.

The US goal is to restore pre-war levels of oil and gas transit through the Strait of Hormuz, US Vice President JD Vance said on Sunday.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello from the DW newsroom in Bonn, Germany, and to our coverage of the war in Iran and developments from across the Middle East. 

One issue we'll be looking at today is a statement from the Iranian Foreign Ministry that it intends to charge commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with a still-unreached agreement with Oman on the future management of the narrow waterway.

entries.title: ASEAN closing ranks as cyberscam threat escalates
entries.summary: Southeast Asian governments are searching for a joint strategy against cyberscammers, a criminal industry that has grown too big, too connected and too embedded in ASEAN economies to be solved just by policing.
entries.content:
August 10, 2026

Southeast Asian governments are searching for a joint strategy against cyberscammers, a criminal industry that has grown too big, too connected and too embedded in ASEAN economies to be solved just by policing.

For years, governments across Southeast Asia largely approached the region's online fraudsters as a matter for the police, anti-trafficking agencies and border authorities.

But these bodies have appearently failed to stem the rise of international cyberscam cartels. The illicit industry is increasingly using international banking systems, cryptocurrencies, telecommunications networks, shell companies and trafficking routes, with some of its centers operating under the protection of armed or politically connected groups.

Now, ASEAN governments seem increasingly willing to tackle the threat as a united bloc.

Myanmar approves death penalty for cyberscam bosses

Signs of this shift were visible at the controversial meeting in Bangkok on August 6 between Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and President Min Aung Hlaing, the head of Myanmar's military government.

The two governments agreed to clamp down on scam centers along their shared frontier, exchange information and jointly disrupt criminal financial flows.

Thailand also offered support for Myanmar's participation in the Egmont Group, an international network of financial-intelligence bodies. Myanmar's military-backed parliament had already voted in favor of applying the death penalty on those caught operating online scam centers.

While visiting Cambodia late last month, Indonesian Deputy Foreign Minister Arif Havas Oegroseno also proposed a joint task force to combat online scam syndicates.

And last week, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Thai Prime Minister Charnvirakul held talks in Jakarta where they agreed their two countries must lead the way and strengthen ASEAN's resilience against scam groups.

Online scams grew into an 'economic security threat'

A UN estimate published last month put the annual losses from cyber scammers — many of whom are located in Southeast Asia — at between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion (between €76 billion and €98 billion) globally in 2025.

Artificial intelligence, cryptocurrencies, encrypted communications and deepfake technology have made their operations cheaper and harder to detect.

"Cyber scams in Southeast Asia have evolved beyond a conventional cybercrime issue and should be viewed as an economic security threat," Hai Luong, a lecturer at Australia's Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice, told DW.

Impact of cybercrime felt around the world

Governments in Southeast Asia have already had to respond to pressure from the US, the EU and China as their online cartels drew international attention.

In October 2025, the US designated Cambodia's Prince Group, one of the country's largest conglomerates, as a transnational criminal organization and imposed sanctions on 146 people and companies connected to it.

US authorities also charged Chinese-born Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi with wire fraud and money laundering conspiracies. Cambodia eventually revoked Chen's citizenship and extradited him to China.

Prince Group's business empire extended across real estate, finance and other sectors in Cambodia. US authorities allege that criminal revenues were mixed with legitimate commercial activities through an international network of companies.

Washington has also sanctioned other Southeast Asian individuals and companies accused of investing in scam compounds and laundering money.

The EU followed last month, imposing sanctions  on Prince Group and Jin Bei Group in Cambodia and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army in Myanmar for alleged involvement in cyberscams.

Cambodia moves against US-sanctioned banks

In 2024, the United States Institute of Peace estimated that Cambodia's cyber-scam industry generated more than $12.5 billion annually, equivalent to roughly a third of the country's formal economy.

The collapse of several scam-linked conglomerates has raised concerns about how the economic shockwaves will affect the rest of the country. At the same time, other voices say negative publicity around scamming is hurting the country's tourism sector and keeping away foreign investors.

Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has acknowledged that the illicit scam economy is damaging legitimate businesses and has vowed a systematic crackdown on online scam networks, including greater scrutiny of the financial sector.

The National Bank of Cambodia has shuttered at least six financial institutions since the start of 2026. Three commercial banks whose licences were revoked in August had all been sanctioned by the US over alleged links to scam networks.

On August 4, the Singaporean government introduced legislation that would expand information-sharing between police and service providers, allow authorities to disable accounts suspected of facilitating scams and strengthen restrictions on financial, telecommunications and online services supplied to suspected offenders.

Criminal groups capitalize on government inefficiencies

As ASEAN nations try to clamp down on cybercriminals, the region's greatest weakness is its fragmentation, Sophal Ear, an associate professor at Arizona State University's Thunderbird School of Global Management, told DW.

"Criminal organizations operate seamlessly across borders while governments continue responding through separate agencies with different mandates and limited coordination," he said.

Ear added that the financial infrastructure used to move and conceal criminal proceeds can often prove more resilient than the law-enforcement architecture designed to dismantle it.

What is in ASEAN's anti-crime plan?

Now, the regional governments seem to be catching on — at least judging by ASEAN's new Plan of Action in Combating Transnational Crime for 2026–2035.

The plan calls for improved intelligence-sharing between national law-enforcement agencies and financial-intelligence units, joint investigations, better cross-border coordination and stronger capacity among anti-money-laundering regulators.

ASEAN has also recently established a joint working group to combat money laundering.

But ASEAN's consensus-based system still heavily relies on national governments implementing those commitments and sharing sensitive financial and law-enforcement information.

"In practice, governments should prioritize disrupting the financial infrastructure, labor supply chains, technological services and transnational business models that sustain scam operations rather than focusing solely on individual offenders," said Luong from Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice.

Moving beyond money mules

Asha Hemrajani, senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, agreed that the region needs to take a "holistic, not siloed" approach to attack the entire cyberscam business model.

"The shared objective should be to identify and dismantle crime syndicate leadership, financial networks and enabling infrastructure, not just arrest money mules or raid individual scam compounds in Cambodia and Myanmar," Hemrajani said.

This includes official scrutiny of high-risk corporate structures and checking sources of funding, as well as a much tougher stance against money laundering, she added. Hemrajani also recommended ASEAN sanctioning business groups linked to the cyberscam networks, similar to how Washington cut off sanctioned Southeast Asian companies from the entire US economy.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: India: Anger over exam irregularities spreads to Jharkhand
entries.summary: Inspired by the Cockroach movement, young people in India's eastern state of Jharkhand are marching on the state assembly to demand transparency and a probe into alleged irregularities in civil service recruitment exams.
entries.content:
India

India: Anger over exam irregularities spreads to Jharkhand

August 10, 2026

Inspired by the Cockroach movement, young people in India's eastern state of Jharkhand are marching on the state assembly to demand transparency and a probe into alleged irregularities in civil service recruitment exams.

Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process.

Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly.

The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters.

The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi.

In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led "Cockroach" protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike.

Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated.

"The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW.

He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).

After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned.

But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs.

What sparked the protests in Jharkhand?

The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July.

Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated.

Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure.

But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem.

What are the protesters' demands?

The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated.

They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery.

The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies.

The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken.

"The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW.

Has the Jantar Mantar playbook spread to the rest of India?

The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers.

That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan .

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters.

But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined.

Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi.

"Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system," Bora told DW. 

"They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future."

Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights.

Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition.

"Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW.

"The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added.

Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12.

"The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment.

Jharkhand's youth wants more from the Ranchi government

The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media, hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession. 

The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission.

But India's youth are refusing to stop there.

Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure.  

For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest.

"We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: UEFA, other football federations unite against Infantino
entries.summary: A few weeks ago, Gianni Infantino looked set for another unopposed term as FIFA president. Now, with an election looming, the beleagured football executive is counting the numbers and could be hanging by a thread.
entries.content:
Europe

UEFA, other football federations unite against Infantino

August 10, 2026

A few weeks ago, Gianni Infantino looked set for another unopposed term as FIFA president. Now, with an election looming, the beleagured football executive is counting the numbers and could be hanging by a thread.

Gianni Infantino's already perilous position as FIFA president took another blow on Monday, as three continental football federations banded together in an apparent attempt to try to force him out.

An "Open Letter to the Football Family" signed by the heads of UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia) appeared to take aim at Infantino —  without actually mentioning him by name.

"This is about something more fundamental: the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it. Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding — or demanding — power to be held," the statement read.

"It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it. When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

The letter criticizes Infantino's now scrapped plan to form a subsidiary arm of FIFA (International Federation of Association Football) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors.

It says that even in withdrawing the plan, FIFA "did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong."

It also labels the plan a "fundamental breach of trust" and lambasted Infantino's seemingly unilateral actions in bypassing the executive FIFA Council for his initial proposal and then holding a summit in Morocco with only selected senior figures within the organization.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness," the letter reads.

The statement comes after media reports that UEFA paid off an alleged mistress of Infantino during his time at the European confederation. FIFA in response criticized "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims" and said that "it is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President."

FIFA have not yet replied to a DW request for comment on the open letter.

What does this change for Infantino?

Were the national federations of the three confederations to fall in line, there would be easily enough votes to oust Infantino at the presidential election in March 2027. FIFA has 211 voting members and thus a presidential candidate in a two-horse race would require 106 votes. UEFA (55 members) AFC (46) and CONCACAF (35) would easily have enough if each confederation's members voted as a bloc.

However, this seems unlikely. While UEFA, who have driven much of the opposition, seem relatively united, the picture in the two other confederations is more mixed. Mexico, one of CONCACAF's most powerful nations and a World Cup 2026 cohost, have backed Infantino while Qatar, who hosted the 2022 World Cup, is one of several Asian nations to have broken ranks.

The South American federation CONMEBOL (10) does not yet have a clear position on Infantino, but one of its most powerful nations, Argentina, have lent Infantino their support. The Oceania federation (11) has also yet to make its position clear.

Perhaps the best news for Infantino was the backing of the African confederation, CAF (54), last week.

A statement from the organization's executive committee said that CAF "unanimously reconfirmed its support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino and thanked him for his support for African Football over the years."

Is there a candidate to challenge Infantino?

This is the big question. As it stands, no candidate has stepped forward. Infantino won the last presidential election unopposed and looked likely to do so again next March, until a few weeks ago.

Though the clear positioning of several confederations against Infantino suggests that running unopposed again is now unlikely, a candidate that can unite those federations in opposition to the Swiss administrator is the next step.

"There's such an imperative to get a candidate who could unite the whole world of football, not just Europe in this case," UEFA vice president, Laura McAllister, recently told DW.

"It's not as easy as people might think. The right candidate has to also have the right level of support," McAllister said. "But if we're talking about the right candidate, then I think that person, that man or woman, needs to be somebody who recognizes that we are simply custodians of the sport and that we look after it and hopefully leave it in better health."

What might happen next?

There will no doubt be plenty of backroom talks about finding a candidate and announcing them at the right time. But given that Infantino retains a reasonable amount of support, football's powerbrokers will likely want to ensure whoever they might put up can win. UEFA executives will likely discuss this at the Super Cup (between the winners of last season's Champions League and Europa League) later this week, while other federations will look to do similar.

Looming in early September is the first FIFA tournament since the controversial sell-off plan was announced. The U-20 Women's World Cup is being held in Poland, a UEFA member, and it is not yet clear whether European teams will participate in the tournament with Infantino still in charge.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Ukrainian drone attack kills at least 13 in central Russia
entries.summary: Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at targets inside Russia, according to Russian officials. The strikes killed more than a dozen in one of Kyiv's deadliest attacks since the Russian invasion began over four years ago.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Ukrainian drone attack kills at least 13 in central Russia

August 10, 2026

Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at targets inside Russia, according to Russian officials. The strikes killed more than a dozen in one of Kyiv's deadliest attacks since the Russian invasion began over four years ago.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk, located in an energy-rich Tatarstan region of central Russia, killed at least 13 people, according to a local press service statement issued Monday.

The attack killed several Central Asians and a child, and wounded 48 more.

Over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border, the region has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has targeted in recent strikes as both sides increase long-range attacks on infrastructure.

The United Nations said such attacks have led to a jump in civilian casualties in Russia and Ukraine.

Unspecified industrial and civilian targets had been hit in Monday's strike, Radmir Belyayev, the mayor of Nizhnekamsk, said in a statement on Telegram.

Russian investigators report that they have initiated a criminal investigation into ​what they say was a terrorist attack.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova accused Kyiv of deliberately attacking civilians.

Ukraine's military ⁠said ⁠it struck the Taneco oil refinery overnight, adding that a ⁠fire was recorded at the site.

The Ukrainian strikes on refineries have led to some fuel shortages and reduced Russia's oil-refining capacity.

Russia has also regularly fired missiles, glide bombs and drones hitting civilian areas in Ukraine and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations.

Later on Monday, Kyiv said special Ukraine drone forces had also struck a Russian petrochemical plant in the Tyumen region.

Kyiv: Air campaign aims to bring Putin to negotiating table

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the campaign aims to force Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the more than 4-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia's war will be felt more and more at their own home — in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday in a social media post.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack.

The Russian Defense Ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. The ministry, however, does not include how many drones or missiles reach their targets or how many were intercepted in the Tatarstan region.

Near the front line in Ukraine, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukrainian officials said.

"On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed," the regional prosecutor's office said in a statement on Telegram.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher
